findings.passage: In 2021, long before the Vatican, he called the possibility of AI systems suffering "a pretty serious issue,"
findings.problem: The Vatican episode, probably the main reason a new reader is searching for him in 2026 (Fortune, June 2026: 'the atheist Anthropic cofounder the Pope chose'), is never mentioned in the opening or the type answer. Yet the body points to it three times before telling it: 'long before the Vatican' (beauty section), 'At the Vatican, as the next section shows, he asked for outside critics' and 'a Vatican stage' (both in 'Why not Type 6?'). A reader without prior knowledge meets an event treated as known, and the Six rebuttal leans on evidence the reader has not seen yet. The orientation gap and the out-of-order evidence both slow the piece where it should be building.
findings.acceptance_test: No sentence mentions the Vatican episode before the reader has been told, in at least one clause, that Olah spoke at the Vatican's presentation of Pope Leo XIV's AI encyclical on May 25, 2026. Either the intro paragraph that begins 'That teenager is now one of the co-founders of Anthropic' gives that dated orientation, or 'The atheist at the Vatican' moves ahead of 'Why not Type 6?'. 'Why not Type 6?' cites no Vatican detail the reader has not already met.

findings.passage: When the G20 summit came to Toronto, police raided the home of a man from HackLab,
findings.problem: The hook gives no date. A reader without context cannot place the Toronto G20, so they can't tell that this happened in 2010, more than fifteen years before the Vatican and Anthropic material, or how it fits the later timeline (first year of university, a year off, the 2012 Thiel Fellowship). The reader has to work out the year from 'He was 18' and a birth year that appears only in the FAQ.
findings.acceptance_test: The first or second paragraph gives the year (2010) for the G20 raid and court support, supported by a source in the evidence record, so the reader can follow the sequence 2010 raid → year off for the trial → 2012 Thiel Fellowship without consulting the FAQ.

findings.passage: And a teenager who is afraid and goes to the courthouse anyway is a textbook counterphobic Six.
findings.problem: Enneagram shorthand that a newcomer can't decode carries part of the argument. 'Counterphobic Six' is never defined, although it is the Six case's best explanation of the hook. 'A 5 wing would fit', 'A Five would be satisfied to understand it' and the bare 'Nines and some Sixes' are also undefined, and 'effective altruism' appears with no gloss. The heart/head/body triad paragraph shows the draft can define terms briefly, but it doesn't do so consistently.
findings.acceptance_test: Every typology term that carries the argument gets a plain-language clause where it first appears (counterphobic = meets fear by moving toward the threat; wing = a neighboring type's influence; Five = the type that pulls back to understand; Nine = the peace-keeping type), or the term is cut. 'Effective altruism' gets a few-word gloss or is rephrased. A reader with no Enneagram knowledge can follow 'Why not Type 6?' and 'What the Four reading leaves out' without leaving the page.

findings.passage: Sad, across contexts and years, even about state misconduct. Rarely angry, rarely suspicious.
findings.problem: The reader has just seen Olah say 'There was a lot of outrage' and 'I'm really outraged at just the appalling ethics of it', in the very security-agency quote this sentence calls 'sad'. 'Rarely angry' therefore reads as contradicted by the article's own evidence, and an attentive newcomer will start to distrust the 'sad' through-line, which is the piece's main discriminator.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence (or the one before it) admits that the outrage is there and makes the narrower claim the evidence supports. For example: outrage appears, but he files it under one hat and lands on sadness, and disappointment is not expressed as suspicion. After the edit, no absolute 'rarely angry' claim conflicts with a quotation already in the article.

findings.passage: Olah only knew him a bit.
findings.problem: The body says Olah 'only knew him a bit', but the H2 'The friend everyone else stepped away from' and the description ('support a friend accused of terrorism') call the man his friend. The description's wording comes from Olah's own 2022 dating doc (S04: 'I dropped out of university to support a friend accused of terrorism'), but the body never quotes that line; it quotes only the second half ('I believe it's most important to support people when others don't'). A reader who arrives from the search snippet finds a weaker relationship and a different charge ('making bombs') than the description promised.
findings.acceptance_test: Body, H2 and description agree on the relationship and the charge. Preferably the body quotes Olah's own 2022 sentence in full, attributed to the dating doc, next to the 'only knew him a bit' detail, so the reader sees he later chose to call the man a friend. Otherwise the description and H2 use the body's framing.

findings.passage: He left to start an interpretability team at OpenAI, and in 2021 joined a group of OpenAI colleagues to co-found Anthropic. Wired calls it "a scary time for him": his immigration status as a Canadian might have been imperiled if the company failed.
findings.problem: Momentum dips at the career pivots that matter most to a newcomer. Distill, the move to OpenAI and co-founding Anthropic share one compressed résumé paragraph that doesn't advance the portrait. The one costly detail (immigration risk) is dropped in without being connected to the article's pattern of doing frightening things anyway, which the hook and the Thiel Fellowship section set up ('a lot of experience in doing things cutting against pressure').
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph either connects the Anthropic founding and its immigration risk to the established pattern (fear acknowledged, moved toward anyway) in one sourced sentence that claims no motive the sources lack, or is trimmed to the facts a reader needs, so the section ends on a portrait point and not a chronology.

protected_passages.passage: The host, Rob Wiblin, assumed he had been driven by outrage. Olah corrected him.
protected_passages.reason: A self-correction like this makes an excellent hook for a newcomer. It sets up the fear-versus-meaning question in one exchange and gives the reader a reason to keep going.

protected_passages.passage: Around then, he walked up to some men who were fishing and "politely asked them how they thought the fish felt about their trade."
protected_passages.reason: A memorable, sourced childhood detail that an unfamiliar reader will retain. It is attributed to his mother, not invented, and the article later brings it back as one of the hidden things he wants seen.

protected_passages.passage: - **2017**, in [Distill's launch essay](https://distill.pub/2017/research-debt/), co-written with Carter: explanation that can "lay bare beautiful insights."
protected_passages.reason: The dated 2017–2026 beauty timeline shows a repeated pattern across a decade at a glance, which makes the motive legible and durable. Keep it as one unit.

protected_passages.passage: Something real is hidden, and he wants it seen and felt. The dog-head circuit, the fish, a model's possible distress. A Five would be satisfied to understand it. Olah wants you to love it, or to grieve it, with him.
protected_passages.reason: This is where the article makes its insight concrete, joining childhood, research and AI-welfare worry in one line a newcomer can repeat. Keep the image even if 'Five' gets a gloss.

protected_passages.passage: It is close to what he says about neural networks. Look long enough at the thing most people walk past, and there is beauty in it.
protected_passages.reason: The ending ties the Gilead quote back to his research without repeating the thesis or tacking on a CTA. It's earned and quiet.

assessment: Read cold, the profile works. The fear-then-courthouse hook creates real curiosity, the intro explains what Anthropic, Claude and interpretability are, the framing question ('safety, or meaning?') can be kept in mind through the whole piece, and a newcomer comes away with surprising, sourced details: the fish, the court support, 'moral loneliness', the date-me doc, Gilead. The stakes stay clear and the ending is earned. The main orientation problem is the Vatican: it is likely why readers are searching now, the opening never mentions it, and later sections treat it as known before the section that tells it. That should be fixed (unfamiliar-01). Smaller problems: an undated hook, undefined Enneagram shorthand ('counterphobic Six', '5 wing', 'Five') where the argument depends on it, a 'rarely angry' claim the quotes contradict, inconsistent friend/terrorism framing between metadata and body, and a résumé paragraph that loses momentum. Body length is about 3,800 words, a little over the 3,500 target, so trims should come from chronology, not evidence. Similarity diagnostic: the tripped pairs (Mike Faist 0.652, Hunter Schafer 0.176) are the triad gloss 'the three types whose core emotion is shame'. That is ordinary type vocabulary, and the next paragraph ties it to Olah's own 'sad' and 'moral loneliness', so I found no meaningful argument reuse. I am keeping the inherited sensitive-allegation (bomb accusation against an unnamed man; unnamed-source Vatican account) and contested-typing risks. I am not escalating further.
